claims.text: A strong low-field magnetocaloric response together with rapid heat exchange, low hysteresis, and mechanical stability is governed by formation of a nanoscale chemically and structurally modulated phase.
Controlled thermo-mechanical processing can produce coherent nanoprecipitates or locally ordered clusters in rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys.
The nanoscale precipitates or clusters modify local magnetic exchange interactions.
The nanoscale precipitates or clusters reduce local magnetocrystalline anisotropy.
The nanoscale modulated regions promote a nearly reversible field-induced transition with a large entropy change at low applied fields.
A continuous, chemically disordered matrix provides high thermal conductivity.
Coherent interfaces between modulated regions and the matrix help maintain mechanical integrity.
The proposed baseline alloy has a relatively homogeneous random-solid-solution microstructure in its as-cast or minimally processed state.
Annealing temperature and time can tune precipitate size, distribution, volume fraction, and coherence without causing coarse phase separation.
Modified exchange interactions and reduced effective anisotropy lower the critical field required for a metamagnetic transition.
Coherent interfaces minimize transition-energy barriers and thereby reduce magnetic hysteresis.
Preservation of a continuous metallic matrix supports rapid heat transfer.
Preservation of a continuous metallic matrix supports mechanical robustness.
Relative to the homogeneous baseline, optimally precipitated samples will have a larger low-field magnetocaloric entropy change.
Relative to the baseline, optimally precipitated samples will have reduced magnetic hysteresis.
Relative to the baseline, optimally precipitated samples will have a faster thermal response during magnetic-field cycling.
Relative to the baseline, optimally precipitated samples will maintain or improve mechanical stability.
The expected enhancement in magnetocaloric entropy change is approximately 10–20%.
The hypothesis is limited to transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys in which nanoscale modulation can be controlled without deleterious coarse phase separation.
Failure to correlate nanoscale modulation with increased low-field entropy change or reduced hysteresis, or degradation of thermal transport and mechanical stability, would falsify the hypothesis.
